allies.rationale_text: Intellectual-humility gives falsifiability the stance needed to expose flaws instead of defend identity.
allies.source_quote: Falsifiability requires intellectual humility - the acknowledging of what you don't know.
allies.affinity_rationale: Canonical states falsifiability 'requires intellectual humility — the acknowledging of what you don't know' — the necessary disposition for genuine self-testing of beliefs.
allies.activation_condition: When testing beliefs requires the willingness to acknowledge ignorance and adopt a student role rather than defending existing positions

allies.rationale_text: First-principles-thinking strips away assumptions and falsifiability pressure-tests whether the rebuilt claim survives contact with reality.
allies.source_quote: First Principles Thinking involves stripping away assumptions and conventional methods to arrive at a set of fundamental facts and desired outcomes. Falsifiability is then used to test the new solutions forged from these fundamental facts.
allies.affinity_rationale: Canonical describes a sequential relationship: first-principles 'strips away assumptions to arrive at fundamental facts' and 'Falsifiability is then used to test the new solutions forged from these facts'.
allies.activation_condition: When solutions built from fundamental facts need to be subjected to rigorous testing to ensure they are grounded in reality rather than untested constructions

antagonists.rationale_text: Confirmation-bias is the psychological enemy of falsifiability because it searches for validating evidence instead of disconfirming tests.
antagonists.source_quote: This bias is the psychological enemy of Falsifiability, as it causes individuals to seek out information that validates their existing beliefs.
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Described as 'the psychological enemy of Falsifiability' — causes individuals to seek validating information rather than the disconfirming evidence that falsifiability demands.
antagonists.activation_condition: When evidence gathering is shaped by the desire to validate beliefs rather than genuinely testing whether they can be disproven

antagonists.rationale_text: Commitment-and-consistency-bias makes it psychologically difficult to accept the evidence that should kill the original hypothesis.
antagonists.source_quote: People have a strong psychological tendency to remain consistent with prior commitments or interpretations. This mechanism fights against the acceptance of disconfirming evidence required by Falsifiability.
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Canonical describes how people 'reduce internal inconsistencies, even if it requires fooling themselves' — the consistency pressure fights against accepting disconfirming evidence.
antagonists.activation_condition: When prior public commitments create psychological resistance to accepting evidence that would require abandoning the original position

structured_tensions.tension_text: Falsifiability conflicts with confirmation-bias when evidence gathering is shaped by the desire to validate the hypothesis rather than genuinely test it.
structured_tensions.source_quote: falsifiability vs confirmation-bias: falsifiability conflicts with confirmation-bias (confirmation bias) when evidence gathering is shaped by the desire to validate the hypothesis rather than genuinely test whether it can be disproven.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Falsifiability conflicts with commitment-bias when prior commitments make it too costly to accept disconfirming evidence.
structured_tensions.source_quote: falsifiability vs commitment-bias: falsifiability conflicts with commitment-bias (commitment and consistency bias) when the desire to remain consistent with prior commitments makes it psychologically difficult to accept disconfirming evidence that would require abandoning the original hypothesis.
